explanation_text: On the stepped rice paddies of the Buyi hillsides, each terrace sits at its own level. Just as every terrace holds its place in the slope, each digit in a number holds a place that determines its value—ones, tens, and hundreds.
image_prompt: Show Guizhou paddy terraces stepped in levels, with each terrace labeled as ones, tens, and hundreds to illustrate place value.

explanation_text: When Buyi villagers pour more rice into a bamboo basket, the amount grows; when rice is scooped out for a meal, it shrinks. These everyday actions are addition and subtraction.
image_prompt: Show a Buyi bamboo rice basket being filled and then partially emptied, with the changing totals labeled above.

explanation_text: For the March Third festival, glutinous rice cakes are laid out in equal rows, showing multiplication. When the same cakes are shared equally among the guests, that is division.
image_prompt: Show rows of glutinous rice cakes arranged evenly on a Buyi table, then divided into equal shares for guests.

explanation_text: Pairs of dancers move together to the beat of the Buyi long drum during festival celebrations. When every dancer has a partner, the number is even; one dancer left alone makes it odd.
image_prompt: Show Buyi festival dancers moving in pairs to the long drum, with one single dancer standing alone to represent an odd number.

explanation_text: Buyi batik cloth is decorated with repeating dot patterns that march in steady steps across the fabric. Following every fifth dot is just like counting by fives.
image_prompt: Show a strip of Buyi batik with repeating dots, every fifth dot highlighted to illustrate skip counting.

explanation_text: Rice baskets stacked in a Buyi home hold different amounts of grain. Comparing their levels shows which number is greater or smaller.
image_prompt: Show several Buyi bamboo baskets with different rice levels, using > and < symbols between them.

buyi_culture: Estimating rice for New Year cakes
explanation_text: When steaming five-color glutinous rice for the Buyi New Year, cooks estimate how much rice and water to prepare. Rounding to a nearby convenient amount works the same way.
image_prompt: Show a cook estimating bowls of rice for five-color glutinous rice, with rounded amounts labeled.

explanation_text: At the March Third festival, a large glutinous rice cake is shared equally among the guests. Each person's portion is a fraction of the whole cake.
image_prompt: Show a round Buyi rice cake cut into equal slices, each slice labeled as a fraction of the whole.

explanation_text: Cutting one rice cake into 2 equal halves or into 4 equal quarters still gives the same total amount. Different-sized parts can name the same portion, like equivalent fractions.
image_prompt: Show a Buyi rice cake first cut into halves, then into quarters, demonstrating equal total portions.

explanation_text: Small bundles of harvested rice can be tied into fewer larger bundles without changing how much grain there is. Grouping the same amount in bigger units is like simplifying a fraction.
image_prompt: Show small bundles of rice being tied into fewer large bundles, labeled with a reduced fraction.

explanation_text: A Buyi household stores three full jars of rice wine and half a jar more. That total is 3½—a whole number plus a fraction.
image_prompt: Show three full rice-wine jars and one half-full jar labeled as 3½.

explanation_text: When rice wine fills more than one jar but is still counted in single-jar units, the total can be written as a fraction greater than one.
image_prompt: Show several small jars of rice wine filling more than one whole jar, labeled as an improper fraction.

explanation_text: Batik makers pour dye from several small bowls into one big vat. Combining these partial amounts makes a whole—just like adding fractions.
image_prompt: Show bowls of indigo dye being poured together into one vat to make a whole amount.

explanation_text: Pouring some rice wine out of a full jar leaves a remaining portion. Removing a part from a whole shows fraction subtraction.
image_prompt: Show a rice-wine jar with part poured out, the remaining amount labeled as a fraction.

buyi_culture: Half of a rice cake half
explanation_text: If each guest at the festival takes half of a half-portion of rice cake, they are finding a fraction of a fraction. That is multiplying fractions.
image_prompt: Show a rice cake divided into halves, and one half divided again into smaller portions.

explanation_text: A portion of cake dough is cut into several smaller equal pieces. Asking how many small pieces fit in the portion is like dividing fractions.
image_prompt: Show a piece of Buyi cake dough being cut into many small equal pieces.

explanation_text: Grain and rice wine are weighed in jin and liang, and measured in liters. A measure like 1.5 liters of rice wine is a decimal number.
image_prompt: Show a measuring container marked 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 liters of rice wine.

explanation_text: Saying half a jin of rice or 0.5 jin describes the same amount. Moving between the two forms is converting fractions and decimals.
image_prompt: Show two baskets of rice, one labeled ½ jin and the other 0.5 jin, holding the same amount.

explanation_text: When a Buyi student scores 90 out of 100 on a mathematics test, that is 90%. Percents express parts per hundred.
image_prompt: Show a test paper with 90/100 written and a 90% mark beside it.

explanation_text: A 10% discount on batik cloth at a Xingyi market lowers the price by a tenth. Finding such a part of a number is the percent of a number.
image_prompt: Show a market stall in Xingyi with batik cloth marked '10% off' and reduced price tags.

explanation_text: In a Buyi storehouse, some jars are labeled with their contents and some are not. An unlabeled jar stands for an unknown quantity—a variable.
image_prompt: Show labeled storage jars (2 jin, 3 jin) and one unlabeled jar marked x.

explanation_text: If a shelf holds 2 known baskets of rice and x more unknown ones, the total is described by the expression 2 + x.
image_prompt: Show two rice baskets plus one unlabeled basket, symbolized as 2 + x.

explanation_text: A Buyi farmer carries two baskets of rice on a shoulder pole. When both sides balance evenly, the weights are equal—like both sides of an equation.
image_prompt: Show a shoulder pole with balanced rice baskets on both ends, labeled as an equation.

explanation_text: If one side of a carrying pole is heavier, the farmer adds or removes rice until it balances. One adjustment solves a one-step equation.
image_prompt: Show a shoulder pole being balanced by adding or removing rice from one basket.

explanation_text: Making batik requires drawing with wax, then dyeing the cloth, then boiling it to reveal the pattern. Each step must follow the last—like solving a two-step equation.
image_prompt: Show the batik sequence: wax drawing, then dyeing, then boiling, as steps to a finished cloth.

explanation_text: One family's paddy field may yield more rice than another's. Comparing harvest sizes shows greater-than and less-than relationships.
image_prompt: Show two paddy fields with different rice yields and > and < symbols between them.

explanation_text: Five-color glutinous rice needs soaking, then coloring, then steaming—the order cannot be changed. Doing operations in the right order is like following PEMDAS.
image_prompt: Show the stages of five-color glutinous rice in strict order, labeled like parentheses, exponents, and multiplication.

explanation_text: When a weaving shuttle wears out, it is replaced with another of the same size. Replacing one thing with an equal one is substitution.
image_prompt: Show a broken weaving shuttle replaced by an identical one on a Buyi loom.

explanation_text: The countless peaks of Wanfenglin rise from the valley near Xingyi, each one marking a position on the land. Each peak is like a point in geometry.
image_prompt: Show the peaks of Wanfenglin with individual summits marked as points on a coordinate grid.

explanation_text: The warp threads stretched tight on a Buyi weaving loom run straight and long. They look like geometric lines that extend in both directions.
image_prompt: Show taut warp threads on a Buyi loom extending straight like geometric lines.

explanation_text: When a wooden window of a stone house is opened, it forms an angle with the frame. The wider the opening, the larger the angle.
image_prompt: Show a stone-house window opened partway with the angle between the frame and window marked.

buyi_culture: Warp and weft on a loom
explanation_text: On a Buyi loom, the warp and weft threads meet at right angles to form the woven cloth. Their crossing shows perpendicular lines.
image_prompt: Show warp and weft threads on a Buyi loom meeting at right angles.

explanation_text: The long stone walls of a Buyi stone village run side by side without ever meeting. They are parallel lines.
image_prompt: Show parallel stone walls of a Buyi stone village running side by side.

explanation_text: Seen from a high hillside, the roofs of a Buyi stone village form many-sided closed shapes. These layouts are polygons.
image_prompt: Show the overhead layout of a Buyi stone village with roofs forming closed geometric shapes.

explanation_text: The gabled roofs of Buyi stone houses slope down to form triangular shapes. Each roof section is a triangle.
image_prompt: Show the triangular gables of Buyi stone houses.

explanation_text: The woven brocade of the Buyi is patterned with squares and rectangles. These four-sided motifs are quadrilaterals.
image_prompt: Show Buyi brocade with repeating square and rectangular motifs.

explanation_text: Walking all the way around the boundary of a Buyi stone village gives its full distance. That distance is the perimeter.
image_prompt: Show a path tracing the boundary around a Buyi stone village with a dashed perimeter line.

explanation_text: A paddy field is measured by how much ground it covers. The size of its surface is the area.
image_prompt: Show a Buyi paddy field shaded to display its area.

explanation_text: Tall grain storage bins in a Buyi home hold the year's harvest. The amount a bin can hold is its volume.
image_prompt: Show Buyi grain storage bins filled to different levels to illustrate volume.

explanation_text: Seen from above, the plunge pool at Huangguoshu Waterfall spreads into a wide circle. Its radius, diameter, and circumference are circle properties.
image_prompt: Show Huangguoshu Waterfall's plunge pool from above with radius and diameter lines marked.

explanation_text: The face of a Buyi bronze drum is a perfect circle. No matter the drum's size, the ratio of its circumference to its diameter is always the constant π.
image_prompt: Show circular Buyi drum faces labeled with circumference and diameter measurements.

explanation_text: On a Buyi loom, the warp threads run one way and the weft the other, forming a grid. Where a thread crosses, it has a position—like a coordinate plane.
image_prompt: Show a Buyi weaving grid with vertical and horizontal threads labeled as x and y axes.

explanation_text: Locating each house in a stone village on a map places it at a specific spot. Marking each spot is plotting points.
image_prompt: Show a map of a Buyi stone village with each house marked as a plotted point.

explanation_text: The batik and brocade patterns of the Buyi mirror themselves across a center line. Each side balances the other—that is symmetry.
image_prompt: Show a Buyi batik or brocade pattern split by a mirror line with matching halves.

explanation_text: During festivals, Buyi dancers turn and shift as the long drum beats. Moving, rotating, and flipping positions are geometric transformations.
image_prompt: Show Buyi circle dancers rotating and shifting to illustrate translations and rotations.

explanation_text: Batik dyers mix indigo paste and water in a fixed balance for the right color. That balance is a ratio.
image_prompt: Show an indigo dyeing vat with dye and water labeled in a ratio like 2:1.

explanation_text: When a brocade pattern is woven larger, every motif grows by the same factor so the design stays true. Keeping that balance is proportion.
image_prompt: Show a small and a large Buyi brocade with identical geometric proportions.

explanation_text: A Buyi weaver counts how many feet of cloth she finishes in one day. That amount per day is a unit rate.
image_prompt: Show a Buyi weaver at a loom with a label of cloth woven per day.

explanation_text: A villager sketches a small map of the large stone village, keeping every distance in the same proportion. That is a scale drawing.
image_prompt: Show a Buyi stone village and a smaller scaled map beside it with a scale legend.

explanation_text: If a family's rice harvest grows from 100 baskets to 120 baskets, that is a 20% increase. Such growth is percent change.
image_prompt: Show rice baskets increasing in number with a +20% label.

explanation_text: After the autumn harvest, Buyi families count how many baskets of rice each field produced. Writing these counts down is data collection.
image_prompt: Show a Buyi farmer recording rice basket tallies on a clipboard.

explanation_text: Villages along the Beipanjiang compare their rice yields season by season. A table or graph makes the comparisons easy to see.
image_prompt: Show a table and bar graph comparing rice yields across seasons.

explanation_text: Finding the average amount of rice each field yields per day shows the mean.
image_prompt: Show a table of paddy yields with the average value highlighted.

explanation_text: When family harvests are arranged from smallest to largest, the middle one is the median.
image_prompt: Show family harvests lined up with the middle value highlighted as the median.

explanation_text: If most fields in the valley are planted with the same rice variety, that variety is the mode.
image_prompt: Show paddy fields with different crops, the most common variety highlighted.

explanation_text: The gap between the biggest and smallest harvest in a Buyi village shows the range.
image_prompt: Show a bar chart with the shortest and tallest harvest bars marked for the range.

explanation_text: Each bar in a chart can show how many baskets of rice one family harvested. Bars make quick comparisons easy.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph labeled by family names with rice harvest totals.

explanation_text: A line graph can show how the water level of Huangguoshu Waterfall changes month by month through the year.
image_prompt: Show a line graph labeled with months and water levels.

explanation_text: A pie chart can show what share of a Buyi village's fields are planted with rice, corn, and vegetables. Each slice is a percentage.
image_prompt: Show a pie chart divided into crop categories with percentages.

explanation_text: At the March Third festival, games of chance decide who receives the embroidered balls and gifts. Estimating the chance of winning is probability.
image_prompt: Show a March Third festival game with probability labels above the possible outcomes.

explanation_text: The geometric borders of Buyi brocade and batik repeat the same motif again and again. These repetitions are patterns.
image_prompt: Show repeating geometric motifs in Buyi brocade borders.

explanation_text: A fixed amount of rice plants always gives a certain number of grains at harvest. Each input produces one output—that is a function.
image_prompt: Show a diagram linking rice bundles (input) to grain counts (output).
